title: GPX Average Speed Calculator: Track Pace Truth
description: Compute average speed from a GPX track's distance and elapsed time with the GPX Average Speed Calculator — elapsed, not moving. Free, local.
summary_sentence: For example, a 10-kilometre track recorded over exactly 2,400 seconds of elapsed time averages exactly 15.0 km/h — including every red light and photo stop inside those 40 minutes.
quick_answer: The GPX Average Speed Calculator combines a GPX track's total distance with the span between its first and last timestamps to give the overall average speed. Load the file locally and read the elapsed-time average — the only average a timestamp range can truthfully produce.

Devices disagree about pause handling. Recompute the elapsed average from the raw file and the argument ends with arithmetic.
Your group's real pace over a trail, stops included, from last weekend's GPX is next weekend's plan — the elapsed average is the planning number.
An absurd average (300 km/h on a hike) flags a corrupt timestamp or a teleporting GPS point before it poisons a training log.
10.00 km over 2,400 seconds: 2,400 s is 0.6667 hours, and 10 ÷ 0.6667 = 15.0 km/h. Every average-speed figure on Earth is this division wearing different data.

faq: How is distance measured between trackpoints?
Great-circle (haversine) distance between consecutive trackpoints on the WGS84 sphere, summed along the track — the same method the route-stats tools on this site use.
What if the GPX has no timestamps?
No span, no average — the file must carry <time> elements on its trackpoints. The Timestamp Span Calculator shows exactly what time data a file holds.
Multiple tracks or segments in one file?
The average spans the file's recorded activity; segments separated by long gaps (an overnight pause) will drag the average hard. Split such files per outing for meaningful numbers.
No — this is horizontal ground speed over elapsed time. Vertical speed is its own curiosity, answered by the elevation tools from the same file.
Kilometres per hour and miles per hour both — cycling and running audiences read different dials, and pace (minutes per unit) lives on the Speed / Pace Helper page.
Why is my average lower than my watch showed?
Almost always pauses: your watch likely auto-paused, the elapsed clock did not. The difference between the two numbers is your stopped time, priced.
